case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Florida’s and Texas’s social-media “must-carry” and viewpoint-discrimination restrictions on platforms’ content moderation violate the First Amendment by compelling or restricting editorial discretion.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Speech Clause) as applied to state laws regulating online platforms’ content-moderation decisions (including Texas HB 20 § 7 and Florida’s challenged provisions in S.B. 7072).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The state petitioners (Florida in Moody; Texas defending HB 20 in Paxton) argue that large social-media platforms function like common carriers or communications conduits rather than speakers, so the states may prohibit viewpoint discrimination and require nondiscriminatory access, characterizing content moderation as censorship of users and asserting the laws permissibly protect the public’s access to speech and prevent perceived bias without violating the platforms’ First Amendment rights.
case_analysis.respondent_position: NetChoice and allied industry respondents argue that platforms’ content moderation and curation are protected expressive/editorial judgments, so state laws that bar “viewpoint discrimination,” impose must-carry obligations, or otherwise constrain moderation are content- and viewpoint-based regulations that trigger heightened scrutiny and are unconstitutional compelled speech; they also contend that labeling moderation as “censorship” is legally irrelevant and contradicts Supreme Court doctrine recognizing editorial discretion.
key_precedents: Miami Herald Publ’g Co. v. Tornillo (1974)
Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, Inc. (1995)
National Institute of Family & Life Advocates v. Becerra (2018)

John Roberts.reasoning: The States’ strongest point remains the “common carrier” analogy, but relabeling cannot overcome that these statutes single out and forbid “viewpoint discrimination” in the platforms’ decisions to display, rank, label, or remove speech—core editorial judgments protected by Tornillo and Hurley. Justice Kavanaugh’s emphasis that the laws are not neutral carriage duties but instead target viewpoint-sensitive moderation reinforces that this is compelled carriage of unwanted speech, not regulation of nonexpressive conduct. Justice Barrett’s observation about the compelled-explanation provisions strengthens the First Amendment defect under our compelled-speech cases (including NIFLA), and it supports a narrow, institutionally modest holding invalidating the must-carry/viewpoint-discrimination and justification mandates as applied to content-moderation decisions. No colleague has offered a doctrinally workable way to uphold these provisions without effectively rewriting or sharply narrowing Tornillo/Hurley, which I am not prepared to do.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The States’ strongest contention—that these platforms are “common carriers” subject to nondiscrimination duties—fails because the statutes’ text does not impose a neutral, across-the-board duty to transmit; it singles out and penalizes “viewpoint discrimination,” i.e., editorial judgments about what speech to disseminate. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, Tornillo forecloses compelled-access regimes that strip a private entity of “editorial control and judgment,” and no common-carrier label can override the First Amendment’s original public meaning protecting a speaker’s right to choose what to publish. Justice Barrett’s point about compelled explanation/justification requirements further confirms that these laws compel speech in addition to compelled carriage, aggravating the constitutional defect rather than curing it. Nothing offered in defense of the statutes supplies a historically grounded basis to treat viewpoint-based moderation mandates as mere regulation of nonexpressive conduct.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The States’ strongest point remains the “common carrier” analogy, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, these statutes are not neutral, across-the-board carriage regimes; they specifically prohibit “viewpoint discrimination” in the platform’s decisions to remove, label, or rank speech, which is quintessential editorial judgment. That places the laws squarely within Tornillo and Hurley: the State cannot compel a private actor to disseminate speech it would otherwise exclude, even if the State believes the actor has outsized market power. Justice Barrett’s observation about compelled explanations adds an independent compelled-speech burden (NIFLA-like) that further confirms the statutes regulate expression rather than merely economic conduct, and as a practical matter invites constant governmental supervision of moderation choices. No colleague has offered a principled doctrinal basis to distinguish these precedents without effectively hollowing them out, so my vote remains for Respondent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The States’ strongest point remains the “common carrier” analogy, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, these statutes are not neutral transmission duties—they directly police and penalize viewpoint-based moderation and ranking, which are editorial judgments protected by Tornillo and Hurley. Justice Barrett’s focus on the compelled-explanation provisions reinforces that the laws burden speech twice over: they compel carriage and also compel the platform to speak by justifying its expressive choices, a concern we have treated skeptically in cases like NIFLA. Pragmatically, constraining moderation predictably increases harassment and threats and reduces access for vulnerable users, underscoring the real-world First Amendment harm of state control over editorial discretion. No colleague has offered a doctrinally coherent way to accept the common-carrier label here without collapsing our compelled-speech precedent into a formality.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The States’ strongest point remains the “common carrier” analogy, but as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, these statutes are not neutral transmission mandates; they trigger on and police “viewpoint discrimination” in hosting, ranking, labeling, and removal—classic editorial judgments under Tornillo and Hurley. Justice Barrett’s emphasis on the compelled-explanation provisions matters for my analysis because it shows the laws don’t just restrict what platforms may do; they affirmatively force platforms to speak in state-prescribed ways about individualized moderation decisions, heightening the First Amendment burden in a NIFLA-like fashion. From a pragmatic textualist lens, accepting the carrier label would require courts (and regulators) to administer a viewpoint-sensitivity regime across billions of moderation actions, an unworkable supervisory project that confirms the laws’ real operation is commandeering editorial discretion. Nothing in the States’ framing supplies a principled way to uphold these provisions without effectively hollowing out Tornillo/Hurley, so my vote remains for the Respondents.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The States’ strongest claim remains the “common carrier” analogy, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, these statutes are not neutral carriage rules; they turn on whether the platform acted on “viewpoint,” thereby regulating quintessential editorial judgment about selection, ranking, and removal. Justice Barrett’s observation about compelled explanations reinforces that the laws do not merely regulate economic conduct—they compel platforms to speak and to justify speech decisions, a burden our compelled-speech cases (including NIFLA) treat with special suspicion. Labeling a speaker a “carrier” cannot overcome the First Amendment’s original guarantee that private parties may decide what they will (and won’t) disseminate, and Tornillo/Hurley squarely forbid this sort of state-commanded access regime. No colleague has offered a principled way to uphold viewpoint-triggered must-carry without effectively overruling or gutting those precedents, so my vote remains with Respondents.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The States’ strongest point remains the common-carrier analogy, but it fails here because, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, these statutes do not impose a historically rooted, content-neutral duty to carry all lawful speech; they instead prohibit “viewpoint discrimination” in the very acts of hosting, ranking, labeling, and removing—core editorial judgments protected by Tornillo and Hurley. Justice Barrett’s focus on the compelled-explanation/rationale requirements further confirms the First Amendment problem: the laws not only compel carriage but also compel the platform to speak on the State’s terms, akin to the compelled-speech concerns we flagged in NIFLA. Even if one could regulate dominant platforms in some narrower, truly neutral carrier-like way, these provisions invite ongoing government supervision of speech decisions at scale, a practical and institutional concern that reinforces why our precedent cannot sustain them. I therefore see no principled path to uphold these laws without effectively narrowing Tornillo/Hurley, which I am not prepared to do.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The States’ strongest contention remains the “common carrier” analogy, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, these statutes are not a neutral, generally applicable duty to transmit; by their text they single out and prohibit “viewpoint discrimination,” thereby directly controlling platforms’ editorial judgments about what to display, rank, or remove—conduct Tornillo and Hurley treat as protected expression. Justice Gorsuch’s point reinforces that relabeling does not change the constitutional character of compelled carriage when the trigger is content or viewpoint, and it would invite courts into ongoing supervision of editorial decisions. I also agree with the Chief (and Justice Kagan) that the compelled-explanation provisions add a distinct compelled-speech burden akin to NIFLA, increasing the chill on moderation and underscoring that the laws regulate speech rather than incidental economic conduct. Nothing raised in conference supplies a principled basis, consistent with original public meaning and our precedent, to uphold these viewpoint-targeted mandates without effectively rewriting Tornillo/Hurley.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The States’ strongest argument remains the common-carrier analogy, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh explain, these statutes are not neutral transmission rules—they are triggered by, and operate on, content- and viewpoint-based moderation decisions, which is exactly what Tornillo and Hurley protect as editorial judgment. Justice Barrett’s point about the compelled-explanation provisions sharpens the First Amendment violation: forcing platforms to generate state-mandated rationales for individualized removals is compelled speech and a procedural burden that predictably chills moderation, consistent with our skepticism in cases like NIFLA. From a progressive-pragmatist lens attentive to procedural fairness and real-world consequences, the regime would invite constant governmental second-guessing of millions of moderation calls, undermining workable governance and worsening harassment risks for vulnerable users. No colleague has offered a doctrinally coherent way to uphold these provisions without effectively rewriting Tornillo/Hurley or accepting pervasive state supervision of private editorial systems.

John Roberts.reasoning: Both Texas HB 20 § 7 and Florida’s S.B. 7072 restrictions operate as content- and viewpoint-based constraints on platforms’ content-moderation choices and, in practical effect, compel carriage of speech the platforms would otherwise exclude. Our precedents treat such editorial judgments—even when they involve selecting and arranging third-party speech—as protected First Amendment activity, and the State generally may not force a private publisher “to publish that which reason tells them should not be published.” Miami Herald Publ’g Co. v. Tornillo, 418 U.S. 241, 256 (1974); see also Hurley v. Irish-Am. Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Grp. of Bos., 515 U.S. 557, 569–70 (1995). Given the breadth of these laws and the centrality of editorial discretion to the First Amendment, the challenged must-carry and viewpoint-discrimination provisions cannot be sustained on the States’ “common carrier” characterization without overruling or sharply narrowing Tornillo and related doctrine, which I would not do absent necessity.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The First Amendment’s text protects “the freedom of speech,” which has long included the right not to speak and to exercise editorial judgment over what to publish. Florida’s and Texas’s must-carry and viewpoint-discrimination prohibitions operate as compelled speech and direct restraints on editorial discretion by forcing platforms to disseminate speech they would otherwise exclude, which Tornillo holds unconstitutional. Nor does relabeling platforms as “common carriers” change the First Amendment analysis where the laws target platforms’ content-based moderation choices rather than impose a neutral carriage duty; Hurley likewise recognizes that compiling and presenting third-party speech is itself protected expression. Because these statutes regulate speech based on content and viewpoint, they are presumptively invalid under the Free Speech Clause.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: However novel the medium, the First Amendment’s text protects a private speaker’s right to decide what to publish, and Florida’s and Texas’s must-carry/viewpoint-nondiscrimination mandates operate as compelled speech by forcing platforms to disseminate expression they would otherwise exclude. Under Miami Herald Publ’g Co. v. Tornillo (1974), the State may not require a private publisher to provide access or a right of reply, and Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, Inc. (1995) likewise protects the choice of what messages to include in a curated expressive product. Texas HB 20 § 7 and the challenged S.B. 7072 provisions single out particular speakers and constrain content-based editorial judgments, triggering at least heightened scrutiny that these laws are unlikely to satisfy. Whatever the practical concerns about perceived bias or market power, recasting platforms as common carriers cannot erase the compelled-publication problem where the statutes regulate the platforms’ own moderation decisions rather than mere transmission.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Texas HB 20 and Florida S.B. 7072’s must-carry and “no viewpoint discrimination” rules regulate platforms’ content-moderation choices—editorial judgments about what to display, prioritize, or remove—and thus compel or restrict speech in violation of the First Amendment. Under Miami Herald Publ’g Co. v. Tornillo, the State cannot force a private publisher to carry speech it would exclude, and Hurley confirms that compiling and presenting the speech of third parties is itself protected expression even when the speaker is not the original author. These laws are viewpoint-based mandates that burden platforms’ discretion to protect users from harassment, threats, and other harms, with predictable real-world impacts on vulnerable populations who rely on moderation for access and safety. Because the statutes intrude on protected editorial discretion and operate as compelled speech, they trigger heightened scrutiny and cannot stand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Texas HB 20 § 7 and Florida’s challenged S.B. 7072 provisions regulate platforms’ content-moderation choices in a way that functions as compelled carriage and viewpoint-based intrusion on editorial judgment, which the First Amendment generally forbids. Under Miami Herald Publ’g Co. v. Tornillo, the State cannot force a private publisher to disseminate speech it would rather exclude, and Hurley confirms that even when an entity curates “multifarious voices,” the selection and arrangement are themselves protected expressive choices. Labeling moderation as “censorship” or calling platforms “common carriers” does not eliminate the First Amendment problem where the laws target the platform’s decisions about what to host, rank, or remove—core editorial discretion subject to heightened scrutiny. Because these provisions are not narrowly tailored to a permissible regulatory objective and instead compel or restrict speech based on content and viewpoint, they are unconstitutional as applied to platforms’ moderation and curation decisions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The First Amendment’s text protects the freedom of speech from state compulsion, and these laws operate as compelled-speech and viewpoint-based restraints by dictating what private platforms must disseminate and forbidding them from making viewpoint-sensitive editorial choices. Under Miami Herald Publ’g Co. v. Tornillo, the State may not force a private publisher to carry others’ messages or surrender “editorial control and judgment,” and Hurley likewise confirms a speaker’s autonomy “to choose the content of his own message.” Labeling platforms “common carriers” cannot by itself erase their expressive editorial discretion where the statutes target content-moderation decisions based on viewpoint, triggering the core First Amendment prohibition on governmental interference with private speech. Because HB 20 § 7 and the challenged provisions of S.B. 7072 compel and restrict editorial discretion in precisely the manner Tornillo forbids, they violate the First Amendment.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Florida’s and Texas’s must-carry and viewpoint-discrimination provisions regulate and compel platforms’ content-moderation choices—quintessential editorial judgments protected by the First Amendment. Under Miami Herald Publ’g Co. v. Tornillo (1974), the State may not force a private publisher to carry speech it would prefer to exclude, and Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, Inc. (1995) likewise protects a private entity’s right to curate and compile others’ speech without compelled inclusion. Labeling platforms as “common carriers” does not overcome the history-and-tradition baseline that governments generally may not dictate editorial discretion, particularly through viewpoint-based mandates that are presumptively unconstitutional. As a practical and institutional matter, allowing States to impose broad must-carry rules on expressive intermediaries would invite unworkable, constant government supervision of online speech and threaten settled First Amendment doctrine.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The challenged Florida and Texas provisions regulate platforms’ content-moderation choices by imposing “must-carry” obligations and forbidding “viewpoint discrimination,” which on their face compel or constrain the platforms’ editorial judgment about what speech to disseminate. Under Miami Herald Publ’g Co. v. Tornillo, the First Amendment generally bars the State from forcing a private publisher to carry speech it would exclude, and Hurley confirms that selecting and arranging third-party speech is itself a protected expressive act even when the speaker is a curator rather than the original author. The statutes’ compelled-explanation requirements (e.g., Florida’s requirement to provide “a thorough rationale” for “censor[ing]” content, FLA. STAT. § 501.2041(2)–(3)) likewise burden editorial discretion and resemble compelled speech concerns addressed in NIFLA v. Becerra. Given that these laws operate as content- and viewpoint-based constraints on private editorial discretion rather than neutral regulation of a common carrier, they violate the First Amendment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Florida’s and Texas’s must-carry and “viewpoint-discrimination” restrictions target platforms’ content-moderation choices—core editorial judgments—and thus operate as compelled speech and viewpoint-based regulation under the First Amendment. Under Miami Herald Publ’g Co. v. Tornillo (1974), the State cannot force a private publisher to carry speech it would otherwise exclude, and Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, Inc. (1995) confirms that curating and compiling third-party speech is itself protected expression. Because these laws single out particular moderation rationales and require carriage or equal treatment of speech the platforms would not choose to disseminate, they trigger at least heightened scrutiny and cannot be justified as mere regulation of “conduits” without undermining procedural fairness and producing serious practical consequences for safe and workable moderation. Labeling moderation as “censorship” does not convert private editorial discretion into state-compellable common-carrier service, and the Constitution does not permit States to commandeer private entities’ speech policies to achieve preferred outcomes.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Florida’s and Texas’s social-media platform laws that restrict or forbid platforms’ content-moderation decisions (including alleged “viewpoint discrimination”) violate the First Amendment by compelling or restricting editorial judgment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Speech Clause), as applied to state laws regulating online platforms’ moderation and hosting decisions (e.g., Texas HB 20 § 7 and Florida’s challenged provisions in SB 7072).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The States (Florida in Moody; Texas in Paxton) argue that major social-media platforms function like common carriers or quasi-public communications infrastructure and therefore may be required to carry user speech without discriminating based on viewpoint; they characterize platforms’ moderation decisions as “censorship” of others’ speech and contend the States may impose nondiscrimination, transparency, and related obligations to protect speakers and the public, analogizing to longstanding antidiscrimination/common-carrier regulation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: NetChoice/CCIA and supporting amici argue that platforms’ decisions about what content to host, rank, recommend, or remove are protected expressive/editorial judgments; laws that compel carriage or prohibit viewpoint-based moderation are unconstitutional compelled speech and content-based regulation, inconsistent with Supreme Court precedent protecting private publishers from forced access/hosting mandates; they also argue that labeling moderation as “censorship” does not negate platforms’ First Amendment rights.
key_precedents: Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo (1974)
Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, Inc. (1995)
National Institute of Family and Life Advocates v. Becerra (2018)

John Roberts.reasoning: The States’ strongest point—Justice Alito’s PruneYard/common-carrier analogy—still cannot account for statutory provisions that impose liability precisely when platforms engage in content- and viewpoint-based removal, ranking, and recommendation, which look like editorial judgment under Tornillo and Hurley rather than mere passive property access. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, the focus on “viewpoint discrimination” is not a neutral access rule but a direct attempt to control the platform’s expressive criteria, and a disclaimer option does not cure compelled carriage when the State is dictating what must be carried and how it may be prioritized. Justice Thomas’s historical point reinforces that relabeling these entities as “common carriers” does not supply a rooted analogue for compelling carriage in a service defined by curation and prioritization of speech. Consistent with minimalism and institutional legitimacy, I would keep the holding narrow—invalidating the core nondiscrimination/anti-moderation mandates as applied to editorial functions—while leaving genuinely severable disclosure or procedural provisions for separate analysis.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The States’ strongest point remains the PruneYard/common-carrier analogy, but it fails because these statutes impose liability precisely when a platform engages in viewpoint-based removal, ranking, or recommendation—core editorial selection about what speech to disseminate. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, that trigger makes this far closer to Miami Herald v. Tornillo and Hurley than to PruneYard or Rumsfeld v. FAIR, where the regulation did not hinge on the speaker’s viewpoint-based publication criteria. Even crediting some historical tradition of nondiscrimination duties for true common carriers, there is no adequate Founding-era analogue for compelling carriage by an entity whose service consists of curating and prioritizing third-party expression, and a disclaimer option cannot cure a law that commandeers editorial judgment. Justice Kagan’s severability point is sound: any genuinely separable disclosure provisions may be evaluated independently, but the core anti-moderation mandates violate the First Amendment as originally understood.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The States’ strongest point remains the PruneYard/common-carrier analogy: dominant platforms look like conduits, and compelled access with a disclaimer can sometimes be permissible. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, these statutes attach liability precisely when a platform engages in content- and viewpoint-based removal, ranking, and recommendation—conduct that functions as editorial judgment under Tornillo and Hurley, not passive property access as in PruneYard or an incidental burden on conduct as in FAIR. Justice Kagan’s severability approach also appeals to my practical-consequences concerns: we can invalidate the core anti-moderation/nondiscrimination mandates that commandeer editorial discretion while leaving genuinely separable notice/disclosure provisions for separate analysis. On this record and text, the viewpoint-focused trigger is the doctrinal flaw that the common-carrier label and disclaimer option cannot cure.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s PruneYard/common-carrier framing is the strongest argument for the States, but it breaks down because these statutes do not impose a neutral access obligation; they impose liability precisely when platforms make viewpoint-laden decisions about removal, ranking, and recommendation—the modern equivalents of editorial judgment. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that is the compelled-carriage problem of Tornillo and Hurley: the State is not merely requiring tolerance of third-party speech, it is commandeering the criteria and outcomes that structure what speech is heard. From a pragmatic perspective, compelling “neutral” moderation predictably forces platforms to carry and algorithmically elevate harassment and extremism, with especially acute burdens on vulnerable users who depend on moderation for safe and meaningful participation. I therefore remain convinced the core nondiscrimination/anti-moderation mandates are unconstitutional as applied to these editorial functions, while any truly severable disclosure provisions could be evaluated separately.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest opposing point remains Justice Alito’s PruneYard/common-carrier analogy, but the statutes’ own triggers make that analogy collapse: liability attaches when a platform engages in viewpoint-based removal, ranking, or recommendation—i.e., the editorial function itself—bringing us squarely under Tornillo and Hurley rather than a passive-access regime. Chief Justice Roberts is right that a disclaimer option does not cure compelled carriage where the State is dictating what speech must be hosted and how it may be prioritized, because the First Amendment injury is the commandeering of editorial criteria, not confusion about endorsement. Nor does FAIR help the States, because there the regulation targeted conduct and any expressive burden was incidental; here, as Justice Barrett notes, the laws specifically police “viewpoint discrimination,” a red flag for government control of private speech. I remain open, on pragmatic/severability grounds, to separately analyzing genuinely informational notice/disclosure provisions if they can operate independently, but the core anti-moderation mandates are unconstitutional as written.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point remains PruneYard and the notion that a dominant platform can be treated like a conduit subject to an access obligation, especially with a disclaimer. But as the Chief Justice Roberts explains, these statutes do not impose a generally applicable access rule; they trigger liability precisely when platforms engage in content- and viewpoint-based removal, ranking, and recommendation—editorial functions that our cases (Tornillo and Hurley) treat as protected speech, not mere property management. Even if one credits some historical regulation of common carriers, I agree with Justice Thomas that there is no rooted analogue for compelling an entity whose product is curated dissemination of others’ expression to carry viewpoints it rejects, and a disclaimer does not cure the State’s commandeering of editorial discretion. I therefore would hold the core nondiscrimination/anti-moderation mandates unconstitutional as applied to those editorial functions, while remaining open (per Justice Kagan) to severability for genuinely informational disclosure provisions if the statutes permit it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s PruneYard/common-carrier framing remains the strongest argument for the States, but it still does not fit these statutes because liability is triggered by the platforms’ content- and viewpoint-based removal, ranking, and recommendation decisions—core editorial judgment under Tornillo and Hurley, not merely passive access to property. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, this is unlike FAIR’s incidental burden on conduct; HB 20 and SB 7072 directly commandeer expressive criteria and outcomes, and a disclaimer option does not cure compelled carriage where the State dictates what must be carried and how it may be prioritized. Justice Kagan’s severability point provides the most institutionally modest path: invalidate the nondiscrimination/anti-moderation mandates as applied to editorial functions while leaving any genuinely separable disclosure provisions for separate analysis. No colleague has supplied a historically rooted common-carrier analogue that would justify imposing nondiscrimination duties on curated expression, so my vote remains to affirm as to the core compelled-carriage provisions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s PruneYard/common-carrier analogy remains the States’ best argument, but it cannot overcome that HB 20 and SB 7072 impose liability precisely when platforms make viewpoint-based removal, ranking, and recommendation decisions—i.e., editorial judgments protected under Tornillo and Hurley. Chief Justice Roberts’ point is decisive for me: the statutes do not merely require access to property; they target and penalize the platform’s expressive criteria, making the disclaimer option inadequate because the First Amendment injury is the commandeering of editorial discretion itself. Justice Kagan’s severability approach also fits my methodology: we can invalidate the core compelled-carriage/nondiscrimination mandates as applied to editorial functions while leaving genuinely separable disclosure/procedural provisions for distinct analysis. On an original public meaning understanding, government control of which viewpoints a private actor must disseminate is at the heart of what the First Amendment forbids, and the “common carrier” label lacks a historically grounded analogue for curated expression.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s PruneYard/common-carrier framing remains the strongest argument for the States, but it still collapses on the statutes’ trigger: liability attaches when platforms engage in viewpoint-based removal, ranking, and recommendation—core editorial functions—so Tornillo and Hurley, as the Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, provide the governing compelled-carriage principle rather than a passive-access analogy. FAIR’s incidental-burden logic does not translate because HB 20 and SB 7072 regulate speech decisions directly, not conduct that only incidentally affects expression. I also agree with Justice Kagan’s severability caution: we should invalidate the nondiscrimination/anti-moderation mandates as applied to editorial judgment while reserving any truly separable disclosure provisions for distinct analysis. The availability of disclaimers, highlighted in PruneYard and by Justice Alito, does not cure the First Amendment injury where the State is commandeering the platform’s expressive curation criteria and outputs.

John Roberts.reasoning: The provisions of Texas HB 20 and Florida SB 7072 that bar or punish platforms’ content-moderation decisions—especially based on viewpoint—operate as compelled carriage and direct restraints on editorial judgment, triggering First Amendment scrutiny. Under Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo, a State may not force a private publisher to disseminate others’ speech or dictate the terms of publication, and Hurley likewise protects a private speaker’s right to choose what messages it will not include. Although the States invoke common-carrier analogies, the laws here regulate expressive curation (hosting, ranking, and recommending) rather than imposing a merely incidental burden of the kind discussed in cases like Rumsfeld v. FAIR, and compelled-speech principles reaffirmed in 303 Creative cut against the statutes. To preserve institutional legitimacy and adhere to precedent, I would resolve the case on the narrow ground that these challenged nondiscrimination/anti-moderation mandates, as applied to platforms’ editorial functions, violate the First Amendment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The First Amendment’s text protects against state laws that compel private parties to disseminate speech they would prefer not to disseminate; there is no Founding-era tradition of treating private speakers who curate or arrange others’ expression as common carriers subject to mandatory carriage. Florida’s and Texas’s prohibitions on so-called “viewpoint discrimination” and their carriage mandates operate as compelled speech and direct restraints on editorial judgment, much like the access mandate invalidated in Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo. Even if States may impose nondiscrimination duties on true common carriers, those historical rules applied to transport and similar services, not to private entities engaged in selecting, arranging, and presenting expressive material, and “no public accommodations law is immune from the demands of the Constitution” when deployed to compel speech. Accordingly, as applied to platforms’ moderation and curation decisions, these laws violate the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The First Amendment does not categorically bar States from imposing nondiscrimination and access obligations on large, open-to-the-public platforms that function in practice as conduits for others’ speech, particularly where the regulations do not prescribe any particular message and are framed as viewpoint-neutral carriage duties. PruneYard Shopping Ctr. v. Robins supports the proposition that a State may require a privately owned intermediary that invites the public in to accommodate others’ speech when the host is not compelled to affirm or be identified with that speech and remains free to disavow it. By contrast, Miami Herald v. Tornillo and Hurley involved entities engaged in their own curated expression where forced inclusion altered the speaker’s message; that rationale applies far less to platforms whose core service is transmitting user expression at massive scale, and the practical consequences of allowing viewpoint-based exclusion by dominant platforms justify the States’ modest access rules. Accordingly, Texas HB 20 § 7 and Florida’s comparable provisions, insofar as they prohibit viewpoint discrimination and impose transparency requirements without compelling endorsement, can be upheld against a facial First Amendment challenge.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Texas HB 20 § 7 and Florida’s challenged SB 7072 provisions regulate platforms’ decisions to remove, rank, and recommend speech and, by targeting “viewpoint discrimination,” operate as content- and viewpoint-based constraints on private editorial judgment in violation of the First Amendment. Under Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo and Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, the State may not compel a private speaker to carry or present speech it would prefer not to disseminate, even when the speech originates with third parties. These laws would predictably force platforms to host harmful or abusive content and deprive users—especially vulnerable communities—of safer access to public discourse, while the proper remedy for perceived unfair moderation is more speech and competition, not state-mandated carriage. Because the statutes directly interfere with expressive curation rather than imposing merely incidental burdens, they resemble the compelled-speech regime condemned in Tornillo rather than permissible regulation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Texas HB 20 § 7 and Florida’s challenged SB 7072 provisions operate as compelled-carriage and viewpoint-based restrictions on platforms’ content-moderation decisions, which are exercises of editorial judgment protected by the First Amendment. Under Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo and Hurley, the State generally may not force a private speaker to disseminate others’ speech or reconfigure its own expressive choices, even when the regulated entity distributes third-party expression. Whatever the States’ asserted “common carrier” framing, these laws target the selection, organization, and prioritization of speech on private platforms, making them content- and viewpoint-based regulations that are hard to square with Tornillo’s forced-access principle and NIFLA’s skepticism of compelled speech. To the extent narrower disclosure or procedural provisions might be severable and evaluated differently for workability, the core nondiscrimination/hosting mandates impermissibly override editorial discretion.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The First Amendment’s text, as originally understood, denies States the power to compel private speakers to disseminate speech they would prefer not to publish, and Texas’s and Florida’s prohibitions on “viewpoint discrimination” in moderation function as compelled carriage of others’ messages. Under Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo, the government may not force a private publisher to print content it rejects, and that principle extends to platforms’ decisions about hosting, ranking, and removing posts—core editorial judgment rather than mere conduct. Nor can the States evade that rule by relabeling platforms “common carriers,” because these laws target content- and viewpoint-based editorial choices, triggering the most exacting scrutiny. To the extent any statutory ambiguity remains, a clear-statement rule grounded in separation of powers and the First Amendment counsels against reading state law to authorize such direct intrusion into protected editorial discretion.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under longstanding First Amendment precedent, a private entity’s decisions about whether and how to disseminate others’ speech are protected “editorial judgment,” and state laws compelling carriage or prohibiting viewpoint-based moderation burden that judgment. Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo and Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston reject compelled access/hosting mandates even when framed as promoting fairness or nondiscrimination, and the same principle applies to platforms’ choices to remove, rank, or recommend content. Texas HB 20 § 7 and Florida’s challenged SB 7072 provisions operate as content- and viewpoint-based constraints on platforms’ expressive discretion, triggering heightened scrutiny that is difficult to satisfy given the direct intrusion on editorial control. Respect for precedent, history and tradition in First Amendment doctrine, and practical workability counsel against converting major platforms into state-imposed common carriers absent a clearer historical analogue and a narrower regulatory fit.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The First Amendment’s original public meaning protects a private speaker’s right to decide what to publish or exclude, and the State may not compel the dissemination of speech or forbid viewpoint-based editorial choices simply by relabeling those choices as “censorship.” Under Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo, a law requiring a private publisher to carry unwanted third-party speech intrudes on “editorial control and judgment,” and Hurley likewise bars compelled inclusion that alters the message of the private host. Texas HB 20 § 7 and Florida’s challenged provisions operate as compelled carriage and content- (indeed viewpoint-) based restrictions on platforms’ moderation decisions, triggering strict scrutiny and conflicting with this Court’s compelled-speech cases (including NIFLA). Precedent does not support treating these platforms as common carriers absent a longstanding, textually grounded tradition of such regulation that is consistent with their expressive, curated presentation of speech.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Texas HB 20 § 7 and the challenged provisions of Florida’s SB 7072, insofar as they bar or penalize platforms’ “viewpoint” moderation and compel carriage of user content, likely violate the First Amendment by intruding on protected editorial judgment. Under Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo, a State generally cannot compel a private publisher to disseminate speech it would not otherwise publish, and Hurley confirms the autonomy of speakers to choose the content of their own message. Treating platforms as quasi-common carriers does not erase their First Amendment interests where the laws target content- and viewpoint-based moderation decisions—core expressive choices about what to host, rank, or remove—rather than neutral, generally applicable conduct regulation. As a matter of procedural fairness and practical consequences, these regimes risk forcing platforms to carry harmful or unwanted speech and chill legitimate moderation, while transparency mandates that demand “thorough rationale” explanations can further burden and distort editorial discretion.
